questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how monsoon winds set the sailing calendar of Indian Ocean traders
questions.stem: In the maritime gallery design brief, you must explain how monsoon winds determined the sailing calendar of Indian Ocean traders.

answer.exemplar: Between June and September the southwest monsoon blows from Africa and Arabia toward India, and from December to March the northeast monsoon blows back the other way. Sailors therefore had to wait at each port for the winds to reverse, so departures followed the seasons rather than the wishes of any ruler.

questions.explanation: The item tests causal explanation of a recurring pattern in the record. A strong answer must name both monsoon seasons, their opposing directions, and the resulting wait at port.
questions.hint: Name the two seasons and the wind each one brings.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why seasonal winds shaped the rhythm of maritime commerce
questions.stem: In the design brief for an Indian Ocean monsoon diagram, you must explain why sailing seasons shaped the rhythm of commerce.

answer.exemplar: Sailing to India and back meant waiting for two separate wind systems in sequence, so a full round trip occupied much of a year and could not be timed at will. Merchants responded by planning departures around the reversal, keeping families and warehouses in port towns for long waits, and favouring goods that would not spoil while they waited.

questions.explanation: The item requires linking wind patterns to practical commercial planning. A strong answer shows how seasonal timing shaped waiting, scheduling and even which goods were traded.
questions.hint: Connect the waiting time to planning.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the practical and social value of legal manuscripts
questions.stem: In the design brief for a manuscript room, you must explain why West African scholarship valued legal texts.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the overall character of long-distance African trade
questions.stem: The design brief for a concluding panel asks which conclusion best fits the evidence of long-distance African trade.

options.text: African trade was local exchange repeated, with no regional or long-distance systems
options.misconception: denies the existence of long-distance systems

options.text: Regional systems were long lasting, profit driven and deeply entangled with religion and learning
African trade depended entirely on outside merchants, with no local participation
options.misconception: erases local participation in trade

options.text: African trade was temporary, ending as soon as states grew strong enough to tax it
options.misconception: assumes states destroyed trade rather than taxing it

questions.explanation: The evidence supports durable, profit-seeking regional systems that also carried scholars, manuscripts and faiths. Local-only exchange, purely outside merchants and a temporary trade all fail.
questions.hint: Weigh durability, profit, and ideas.
